Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) -- The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is working with public health officials in 42 states to determine the cause of an outbreak of a particular type of salmonella called Typhimurium. Salmonella bacteria are transmitted to humans by eating contaminated foods. According to CDC sources, at least 388 people have been infected with this strain since September 3, but most cases occurred between October 1 and December 31, the disease agency said. About 18 percent of cases were hospitalized as a result of their illness, and patients have ranged from two months to 98 years of age. California is reporting the highest case count with 55, followed by Ohio with 53 cases, Massachusetts with 39, Minnesota with 30 and Michigan with 20. The other 37 states are each reporting anywhere from one to 19 cases. The eight states that have not reported any cases connected to the outbreak are Montana, New Mexico, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina, Florida, Alaska and Hawaii. King Nut peanut butter was identified as the source of an outbreak that may have contributed to one death in Minnesota, state public health officials said Friday in a news release. CNN was unable to reach the company for comment. CDC has not identified what food or foods might be causing this outbreak. CDC officials and state public health workers are conducting case control studies, which means they're tracking down people who have been infected as early as September to determine what they may have consumed, to find a common cause.  Learn more about salmonella » . The Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Department of Agriculture are in contact with the CDC, but without a determination of the cause of the outbreak, their involvement is limited. Various strains of salmonella have been linked to previous outbreaks, caused by contaminated eggs, meat, poultry, vegetables, pet food and even peanut butter. Contaminated tomatoes were blamed for a salmonella Typhimurium outbreak in fall 2006, which sickened at least 183 people in 21 states. Most of the victims had diarrhea and fever for about a week. Nobody died in that outbreak. Salmonella infections are caused by bacteria and if necessary can be treated with antibiotics, although some strains have become resistant to these drugs, according to the CDC Web site. Most people infected will develop diarrhea, fever and abdominal cramps within a few days of infection, and their illness can last up to a week. Most recover without any treatment, but some may suffer dehydration and in severe cases require hospitalization. The youngest and oldest patients and chronically ill people with compromised immune systems are at highest risk for severe complications, according to the National Institutes of Health. Until a cause of the outbreak is confirmed, the CDC is recommending the following: . Consumers should thoroughly cook meats, poultry and eggs. They should also avoid consuming raw or unpasteurized milk and other dairy products. Produce should be thoroughly washed as well. Avoid cross-contamination of uncooked meats and produce to prevent spreading any potential salmonella. Frequent washing of hands during food preparation can also help reduce cross-contamination.

ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) — The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is collaborating with health authorities in 42 states as they investigate what is behind an outbreak involving a specific salmonella strain known as Typhimurium.

Salmonella bacteria infect people through the consumption of tainted food. CDC sources said that since September 3, at least 388 individuals have become ill from this strain, though the agency noted that most reported illnesses happened between October 1 and December 31.

Roughly 18 percent of those infected required hospitalization. Patients have been as young as two months old and as old as 98.

California has reported the largest number of cases, with 55. Ohio follows with 53, Massachusetts with 39, Minnesota with 30 and Michigan with 20. The remaining 37 affected states have each recorded between one and 19 cases.

Eight states have not reported any outbreak-related illnesses: Montana, New Mexico, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina, Florida, Alaska and Hawaii.

On Friday, Minnesota public health officials said in a news release that King Nut peanut butter had been identified as the source of an outbreak that may have played a role in one death in the state. CNN was not able to contact the company for a response.

The CDC has not yet determined which food or foods may be responsible for the broader outbreak. Federal and state health investigators are carrying out case-control studies, which involve locating people infected as far back as September and reviewing what they ate in an effort to identify a shared source.

The Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Department of Agriculture have been communicating with the CDC, but their roles remain limited until the cause of the outbreak is established.

Past outbreaks involving different salmonella strains have been traced to contaminated eggs, meat, poultry, vegetables, pet food and even peanut butter. In the fall of 2006, contaminated tomatoes were linked to a salmonella Typhimurium outbreak that sickened at least 183 people across 21 states. Most patients in that outbreak experienced diarrhea and fever for about a week, and no deaths were reported.

Salmonella illness is caused by bacteria and, when needed, may be treated with antibiotics. However, the CDC’s Web site notes that some strains have developed resistance to those medications.

Most infected people develop diarrhea, fever and stomach cramps within several days of exposure, and symptoms can continue for up to a week. Many recover without medical care, but dehydration can occur, and severe cases may require hospitalization.

According to the National Institutes of Health, the greatest risk of serious complications is among very young patients, elderly patients and people with chronic illnesses or weakened immune systems.

Until the outbreak’s source is confirmed, the CDC advises consumers to cook meat, poultry and eggs thoroughly. People should also avoid raw or unpasteurized milk and other dairy products. Fruits and vegetables should be washed carefully. To reduce the chance of spreading possible salmonella, raw meats should be kept from contaminating produce, and hands should be washed often during food preparation.

## CDC investigates multistate Salmonella outbreak sickening 388 people in 42 states

Federal health officials are investigating a multistate outbreak of *Salmonella Typhimurium* that has sickened 388 people across 42 states, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said.

The CDC said investigators are working with state and local health departments to determine the source of the outbreak. While no single contaminated product has been confirmed, officials are reviewing patient interviews, purchase records and laboratory data to identify possible links. Suspected sources in Salmonella outbreaks often include contaminated food products, contact with backyard poultry, reptiles or other animals, and cross-contamination in kitchens.

The agency said illnesses have been reported in the following states: **[insert CDC state-by-state case counts here]**. Health officials caution that the true number of people sickened is likely higher than the reported total because many people recover without medical care and are never tested for Salmonella.

Symptoms of Salmonella infection usually begin six hours to six days after swallowing the bacteria, according to the CDC. Most people develop diarrhea, fever and stomach cramps, and recover without treatment within four to seven days.

However, some people — including children younger than 5, adults 65 and older, and those with weakened immune systems — are at higher risk for severe illness. In some cases, the infection can spread from the intestines to the bloodstream and require hospitalization or antibiotic treatment.

The CDC is urging consumers to take basic food-safety precautions while the investigation continues:

- Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water before preparing food, after handling raw meat, poultry or eggs, and after touching animals or their environments.
- Cook poultry, ground meats and egg dishes to safe internal temperatures.
- Keep raw foods separate from ready-to-eat foods.
- Wash cutting boards, utensils and countertops after they touch raw foods.
- Refrigerate perishable foods promptly.
- Avoid preparing food for others if you have diarrhea or symptoms of a stomach illness.

If the outbreak is linked to animals, health officials also recommend washing hands after touching poultry, reptiles, amphibians or pet habitats, and keeping those animals away from areas where food is prepared or eaten.

People who develop severe symptoms — including bloody diarrhea, diarrhea lasting more than three days, a fever higher than 102 degrees Fahrenheit, signs of dehydration, or repeated vomiting — should contact a health care provider, the CDC said.

**ATLANTA, Georgia — January 18, 2009** — Federal health officials are investigating a multistate outbreak of *Salmonella* infections that may be linked to peanut butter distributed by King Nut Companies, a supplier whose products are used primarily by institutions such as nursing homes, schools, hospitals and food-service operations.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the outbreak involves *Salmonella enterica* serotype Typhimurium, a strain that can cause serious gastrointestinal illness and, in vulnerable patients, potentially life-threatening complications.

According to the CDC, hundreds of people have been sickened across dozens of states. As of the latest federal update, the agency reported **more than 470 illnesses in at least 43 states**, with **several deaths** under investigation as possibly associated with the outbreak. Health officials cautioned that the number of cases may rise as state laboratories continue to identify infections and report them to the CDC.

Investigators from the CDC, the Food and Drug Administration and state health departments are focusing in part on **King Nut brand peanut butter**, after the product was found to contain the outbreak strain of *Salmonella*. King Nut has issued a recall of peanut butter distributed under its name, and officials said the product was manufactured by Peanut Corporation of America at a Georgia facility.

### States Reporting Illnesses

The outbreak has affected people across much of the country. States reporting cases include, among others, **California, Colorado, Connecticut, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia and Wisconsin**, with additional states reporting smaller numbers of confirmed cases.

Health officials said many of the illnesses occurred in people who ate food prepared in institutional settings. King Nut peanut butter is not generally sold directly to consumers in grocery stores, but officials warned that it may have been served in cafeterias, long-term care facilities and other food-service locations.

### Symptoms and Health Risks

*Salmonella* infection typically causes **diarrhea, fever, abdominal cramps, nausea and vomiting** within 12 to 72 hours after exposure. Most otherwise healthy people recover within four to seven days without treatment.

However, the CDC said the infection can be severe in:

- **Infants and young children**
- **Older adults**
- **Pregnant women**
- **People with weakened immune systems**
- **Residents of nursing homes or hospitals**

In serious cases, the bacteria can spread from the intestines into the bloodstream, leading to hospitalization or death if not treated promptly with antibiotics.

People who develop severe diarrhea, bloody stools, high fever, signs of dehydration or symptoms lasting more than several days are urged to seek medical care.

### Recall and Investigation

King Nut Companies has recalled peanut butter distributed under the **King Nut** label and advised customers to stop using it immediately. Federal investigators are tracing distribution records to determine where the peanut butter was shipped and whether other peanut-containing products may have been contaminated.

The FDA said it is inspecting the manufacturing facility and reviewing production and sanitation records. Officials said the investigation remains ongoing and that additional recalls could be announced if other products are linked to the outbreak.

### Food Safety Recommendations

Public health authorities recommend that consumers, food-service workers and institutions take the following precautions:

- **Do not eat or serve recalled King Nut peanut butter.**
- **Check inventory** in schools, nursing homes, hospitals, restaurants and cafeterias for recalled products.
- **Discard recalled peanut butter safely** in a sealed container so it cannot be eaten by people or animals.
- **Wash hands thoroughly** after handling any recalled product or containers.
- **Clean and sanitize surfaces, utensils and storage areas** that may have come into contact with the peanut butter.
- **Avoid cross-contamination** by keeping ready-to-eat foods away from potentially contaminated products.
- **Report suspected illness** to a health care provider or local health department.

The CDC said consumers with questions about whether a peanut product is affected should check recall notices from the FDA or contact the manufacturer. Health officials emphasized that national-brand peanut butter sold in jars at retail stores had not, at this stage of the investigation, been identified as the primary source.

“This remains an active and rapidly evolving investigation,” federal health officials said. “The priority is to identify contaminated products, remove them from distribution and prevent additional illnesses.”

# CDC traced 2008 Salmonella outbreak to peanut products, prompting one of the largest food recalls in US history

*By CNN Health staff*  
*Historical report*

A multistate Salmonella outbreak that began in late 2008 sickened hundreds of people across the United States and was eventually linked by federal investigators to peanut products made by the Peanut Corporation of America, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The outbreak, involving the strain *Salmonella enterica* serotype Typhimurium, was first detected through routine public health surveillance after state laboratories reported genetically similar infections to PulseNet, the national database used to identify foodborne illness clusters.

By the time the investigation was well under way in early 2009, the CDC reported more than 700 illnesses in 46 states. About one-quarter of patients for whom information was available were hospitalized, and several deaths were reported among people infected with the outbreak strain.

## Patients ranged from infants to older adults

CDC investigators said patients ranged in age from less than 1 year old to 98 years old. The median age was in the teens, showing that children and young people made up a substantial portion of reported cases, though illnesses occurred across all age groups.

Health officials said hospitalization was more common among people at higher risk for severe salmonellosis, including older adults, infants and people with weakened immune systems.

Symptoms of Salmonella infection typically include diarrhea, fever and abdominal cramps that develop 12 to 72 hours after exposure. Most people recover without treatment, but severe cases can lead to dehydration, bloodstream infection and hospitalization.

## Investigation pointed to peanut butter and peanut paste

The investigation initially focused on peanut butter served in institutional settings, including nursing homes, schools and hospitals. Epidemiologic interviews found that many patients had eaten peanut-containing products before becoming ill.

The CDC, working with state health departments and the US Food and Drug Administration, later linked the outbreak to peanut butter and peanut paste produced at Peanut Corporation of America’s facility in Blakely, Georgia. Those ingredients were not generally sold directly to consumers in jars, but they were used in a wide range of foods, including crackers, cookies, snack bars, candy and other processed products.

As the investigation expanded, hundreds of companies recalled thousands of peanut-containing products. The recall became one of the largest food recalls in US history.

## What consumers were told to do

Federal health officials urged consumers not to eat recalled peanut-containing products and to check FDA recall lists for specific brands and lot numbers.

Consumers were advised to:

- Throw away recalled peanut products, even if some of the product had already been eaten without illness.
- Avoid tasting products to see if they were safe.
- Wash hands, utensils, shelves and surfaces that may have touched recalled foods.
- Seek medical care for severe diarrhea, high fever, bloody stools, signs of dehydration or symptoms in high-risk individuals.
- Report suspected foodborne illness to local health departments.

The CDC also reminded consumers that Salmonella can survive in low-moisture foods such as peanut butter and peanut paste, making contamination especially concerning when tainted ingredients are distributed widely.

The outbreak underscored the importance of rapid disease surveillance, product tracing and coordinated recalls, public health officials said, as investigators connected illnesses reported across the country to a common source in the food supply.

Epidemiologic work linked illnesses to peanut products, especially **King Nut brand creamy peanut butter**, which was distributed mainly to institutions such as schools, hospitals, nursing homes, and food-service facilities rather than sold directly to consumers.

Key points from the investigation:

- **Outbreak scope:** Hundreds of people were infected across 42 states, with many hospitalizations reported.
- **Minnesota death:** Minnesota health officials reported a death in an infected patient, helping draw attention to the severity of the outbreak and prompting intensified traceback and laboratory work.
- **King Nut peanut butter:** Investigators found Salmonella in an open container of King Nut peanut butter collected from a facility. King Nut recalled its peanut butter after evidence suggested it was a likely vehicle for infection.
- **Case-control studies:** CDC and state health departments used case-control studies—comparing foods eaten by sick people with foods eaten by similar people who were not sick—to identify foods statistically associated with illness. These studies supported peanut butter/peanut-containing products as the likely source.
- **Traceback:** The investigation traced implicated peanut products back through distribution channels to a peanut-processing source, leading to broader recalls of peanut butter and peanut-containing foods.
- **Previous outbreaks:** The CDC noted that peanut butter and peanut products had caused earlier Salmonella outbreaks, showing that low-moisture foods can still harbor Salmonella and cause widespread illness when contaminated.

**Symptoms of Salmonella infection** typically include diarrhea, fever, and abdominal cramps beginning 12 to 72 hours after exposure. Illness usually lasts 4 to 7 days. Severe disease is more likely in infants, older adults, pregnant people, and people with weakened immune systems.

**Treatment** is usually supportive: drinking fluids and replacing electrolytes. Antibiotics are generally reserved for severe cases or high-risk patients because most people recover without them.

**Prevention steps** include:

- Do not eat recalled peanut butter or recalled peanut-containing products.
- Check recall lists and discard or return affected products.
- Wash hands, utensils, and surfaces after handling suspect foods.

- Seek medical care for severe diarrhea, high fever, dehydration, bloody stools, or illness in high-risk individuals.

counterfactuals.output:
## Nationwide Salmonella Typhimurium outbreak under investigation as health officials search for food source

Public health officials are investigating a nationwide outbreak of **Salmonella Typhimurium**, a strain of Salmonella bacteria that can cause diarrhea, fever, stomach cramps and, in some cases, severe illness requiring hospitalization.

The outbreak has been described as **multistate**, meaning illnesses have been reported in more than one state and may be linked by laboratory testing, food-history interviews or traceback investigations. Federal and state investigators are working to determine whether the infections are tied to a common food product, supplier, restaurant chain or distribution source.

### What is being investigated?

Investigators typically use three main tools in Salmonella outbreak investigations:

1. **Patient interviews** — asking sick people what they ate in the week before symptoms began.  
2. **Traceback** — following foods back through grocery stores, distributors, farms or processing facilities.  
3. **Laboratory testing** — comparing bacteria from patients and food or environmental samples using genetic sequencing.

At this stage, officials may be examining several possible food sources, including foods that have commonly caused Salmonella Typhimurium outbreaks in the past, such as:

- **Fresh produce**, including leafy greens, herbs, tomatoes, cucumbers, sprouts and melons  
- **Poultry**, especially raw or undercooked chicken or turkey  
- **Eggs and egg-containing foods**  
- **Ground meat or processed meats**  
- **Unpasteurized milk or dairy products**  
- **Nut butters or other shelf-stable foods**  
- **Foods prepared in shared kitchens**, where cross-contamination can occur

Health officials have not always been able to identify a single contaminated food early in an investigation. Because many Salmonella cases are never tested or reported, the true number of people sick is usually higher than the official case count.

### States reporting cases

In a nationwide outbreak, cases may be reported across multiple regions of the country. State health departments and the CDC generally publish a list of affected states once cases are confirmed through laboratory testing and linked genetically to the outbreak strain.

If you are preparing this as a time-sensitive news item, the state list should be verified against the latest CDC or state health department outbreak notice before publication. The official list may change as new cases are reported and older cases are linked through lab testing.

### Symptoms of Salmonella infection

Most people infected with Salmonella develop symptoms **6 hours to 6 days after exposure**. Common symptoms include:

- Diarrhea, sometimes severe  
- Fever  
- Stomach cramps  
- Nausea or vomiting  
- Headache or body aches

Illness usually lasts **4 to 7 days**, and many people recover without antibiotics. However, Salmonella can be dangerous for:

- Children under 5  
- Adults 65 and older  
- Pregnant people  
- People with weakened immune systems  
- People taking medications that reduce stomach acid

Seek medical care if you have:

- Diarrhea lasting more than 3 days  
- Bloody diarrhea  
- A fever higher than 102°F  
- Signs of dehydration, such as dizziness, dry mouth or little urination  
- Persistent vomiting that prevents keeping fluids down

### How people can reduce the risk of infection

While investigators work to identify the source, public health officials recommend basic food-safety steps to prevent Salmonella infection.

#### Wash hands and surfaces

- Wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds before preparing food, after handling raw meat or eggs, after using the bathroom and after touching animals.  
- Clean cutting boards, knives, counters and plates after they contact raw foods.

#### Avoid cross-contamination

- Keep raw meat, poultry, seafood and eggs separate from produce and ready-to-eat foods.  
- Use separate cutting boards for raw meat and fresh foods.  
- Never place cooked food on a plate that held raw meat unless it has been washed.

#### Cook foods thoroughly

Use a food thermometer. Cook to:

- **165°F** for poultry  
- **160°F** for ground beef and egg dishes  
- **145°F** for whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb and fish, followed by rest time where recommended

#### Handle produce safely

- Rinse fruits and vegetables under running water before eating, cutting or cooking.  
- Scrub firm produce such as melons and cucumbers.  
- Refrigerate cut fruit and vegetables within 2 hours, or within 1 hour if food is exposed to temperatures above 90°F.

#### Avoid high-risk foods

People at higher risk of severe illness should avoid:

- Raw or undercooked eggs  
- Raw milk or unpasteurized dairy products  
- Raw sprouts  
- Undercooked poultry or meat  
- Unpasteurized juices

### What to do if you think you are sick

Anyone with symptoms of Salmonella infection should stay hydrated and contact a health care provider if symptoms are severe. People should also report suspected foodborne illness to their local health department, especially if they believe they became sick after eating a specific food, visiting a restaurant or attending an event.

Public health officials urge consumers not to throw away packaging, receipts or leftover food if they suspect a product made them sick. Those items can help investigators trace the source of an outbreak.

### Bottom line

The Salmonella Typhimurium outbreak remains under investigation, and officials are working to identify the contaminated food source. Until more is known, consumers can lower their risk by practicing careful handwashing, preventing cross-contamination, cooking foods to safe temperatures and handling produce safely. Updates from the CDC, FDA, USDA and state health departments should be monitored as case counts, affected states and product warnings may change.
